nodes.name: In-situ electrodeposition of Ni-Fe-RE LDH
nodes.procedure: In-situ electrodeposition strategy to synthesize Ni-Fe-RE layered double hydroxide precursors uniformly grown on carbon cloth (CC), where RE = La, Ce, Pr, and Nd. The phase information (JCPDS No. 40-0215) and morphology structures of precursors indicate that Ni-Fe-Ce LDH with nanosheets structure was uniformly grown on the carbon cloth (CC).
nodes.source_text: various Ni-Fe-RE-P/CC (RE = La, Ce, Pr, and Nd) self-supporting electrodes were synthesized via one in-situ strategy (Fig. 2a and Fig. S1)... The phase information (JCPDS No. 40-0215) and morphology structures of precursors are shown in Figs. S2 and S3, indicating that Ni-Fe-Ce layered double hydroxide (Ni-Fe-Ce LDH) with nanosheets structure was uniformly grown on the carbon cloth (CC)

nodes.name: Electrodeposition of Ni-Fe LDH
nodes.procedure: Electrodeposition to grow Ni-Fe layered double hydroxide (Ni-Fe LDH) with nanosheets structure uniformly on the carbon cloth (CC).
nodes.source_text: X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) patterns of Ni-Fe-Ce LDH/CC and Ni-Fe LDH/CC are shown in Fig. S7.

nodes.procedure: Ni-Fe-P/CC was obtained by phosphorization using the Ni-Fe LDH/CC as precursor.
nodes.source_text: Ni-Fe-Ce-P/CC was then obtained by phosphorization in Ar atmosphere using the Ni-Fe-Ce LDH/CC as precursor. Both Ni-Fe-P/CC and Ni-Fe-Ce-P/CC electrodes display nanosheets morphology.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni-Fe-Ce-P/CC displays nanosheets morphology with rough surface.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Both Ni-Fe-P/CC and Ni-Fe-Ce-P/CC electrodes display nanosheets morphology (Fig. 2c and d and Fig. S4), while the surface of Ni-Fe-Ce-P/CC became rough.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni-Fe-Ce-P shows nanosheet structure with elemental mapping confirming uniform distribution of P, Fe, Ce, and Ni.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Fig. 2(g and h) exhibits that P, Fe, Ce, and Ni elements are distributed throughout the Ni-Fe-Ce-P nanosheets.

properties.description: Four-panel fluorescence or elemental mapping image

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni-Fe-Ce-P displays lattice fringes with spacing of 0.288 nm corresponding to (111) plane of pyrite Ni2P; Ni-Fe-P shows 0.286 nm.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In Fig. 2(e), Ni-Fe-Ce-P/CC displays distinct lattice fringes with a lattice spacing of 0.288 nm corresponding to the (111) plane of pyrite Ni2P (JCPDS No. 03-0953).

nodes.characterization_summary: All diffraction peaks indexed to pyrite Ni2P (JCPDS No. 03-0953); Ni-Fe-Ce-P peaks show slight negative shift compared to Ni-Fe-P due to Ce doping.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns (Fig. 3a) show all other diffraction peaks of Ni-Fe-Ce-P and Ni-Fe-P samples are indexed to pyrite Ni2P (JCPDS No. 03-0953).

nodes.characterization_summary: Characteristic modes Eg and Ag at 284.6 and 441.1 cm⁻¹ attributed to Ni2P in both Ni-Fe-Ce-P and Ni-Fe-P.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Raman spectroscopy (Fig. 3b) displays that the characteristic modes Eg and Ag (284.6 and 441.1 cm⁻¹) are attributed to Ni2P in Ni-Fe-Ce-P and Ni-Fe-P.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni 2p peaks shift toward lower binding energies after Ce doping (Ni peaks at 852.6/869.8 eV for Ni⁰); increased Ni⁰ content; Fe 2p shows Fe⁰ at 706.3/717.9 eV; Ce 3d shows Ce³⁺/Ce⁴⁺ coexistence; P 2p at 129.6/130.5/134.1 eV.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In comparison with Ni-Fe-P/CC without Ce doping, the Ni peaks of Ni-Fe-Ce-P/CC shift toward lower binding energies, which means the decreased valence state of partial Ni due to the electrons transfer form Ce to Ni. It is also worth noting that the content of Ni⁰ increases after Ce doping.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni K-edge XANES of Ni-Fe-Ce-P shows slight shift to lower energy compared to Ni-Fe-P, indicating decreased Ni valence state.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Compared with Ni-Fe-P, a slight shift of Ni K-edge XANES peak to the lower energy is detected after Ce doping in Fig. 3(h).

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni-P peak at 1.66 Å in Ni-Fe-Ce-P vs 1.63 Å in Ni-Fe-P, confirming lattice distortion from Ce doping.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Fig. 3(i) displays the clear formation of Ni–P bonds, in which the Ni–P peak in Ni-Fe-Ce-P/CC is located at 1.66 Å, while the Ni–P peak in Ni-Fe-P/CC is located at 1.63 Å.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni-Fe-Ce-P/CC shows Rct = 2.2 Ω for OER and 3.0 Ω for HER; Ni-Fe-P/CC shows 3.7 Ω for OER and 4.0 Ω for HER.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The charge transfer resistance (Rct) value of Ni-Fe-Ce-P/CC electrode (2.2 Ω) is less than that of Ni-Fe-P/CC (3.7 Ω)... the Rct of the Ni-Fe-Ce-P/CC (3.0 Ω) was lower than that of Ni-Fe-P/CC (4.0 Ω).

nodes.characterization_summary: Cdl = 7.4 mF cm⁻² for OER and 17.2 mF cm⁻² for HER on Ni-Fe-Ce-P/CC vs 5.7 mF cm⁻² and 14.7 mF cm⁻² on Ni-Fe-P/CC.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The Ni-Fe-Ce-P/CC has a slightly higher Cdl of 7.4 mF cm⁻² than Ni-Fe-P/CC (5.7 mF cm⁻²)... the Ni-Fe-Ce-P/CC possesses larger Cdl (17.2 mF cm⁻²) than Ni-Fe-P/CC (14.7 mF cm⁻²).

nodes.characterization_summary: EDS confirms presence of Ni, Fe, Ce, and P elements in Ni-Fe-Ce-P/CC consistent with XPS.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The presence of Ni, Fe, Ce, and P elements in Ni-Fe-Ce-P/CC catalyst can be detected by XPS spectrum shown in Fig. 3(c), which is in agreement with the energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) results (Fig. S8 and Table S1).
